preamble: Rett Syndrome  |  MECP2-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder  |  Classic RTT (Neul 2010 Criteria)  (OMIM 312750)

questions.domain: Apparently normal psychomotor development in the first 6–18 months of life?
questions.question: Yes – early development appears normal; parents may note subtle differences retrospectively

questions.domain: Subtle developmental stagnation or slowing noted before overt regression?
questions.question: Yes – early Stage 1 stagnation; reduced eye contact, social disengagement, hand interest decline

questions.domain: Deceleration of head circumference growth (acquired microcephaly) after birth?
questions.question: Yes – postnatal head circumference deceleration; acquired microcephaly in majority

questions.domain: Female sex (classic RTT affects females almost exclusively)?
questions.question: Yes – classic RTT occurs predominantly in females; 1 in 10,000–20,000 live female births

sections.heading: REGRESSION PHASE — REQUIRED CRITERION (Stage 2: Age 1–4 Years)

questions.domain: Clear period of regression — loss of skills after a period of normal development?
questions.question: Yes – regression is the cardinal required criterion; must follow demonstrated normal period

questions.domain: Regression onset between ages 1–4 years (typically 12–36 months)?
questions.question: Yes – regression most commonly begins in second year of life

questions.domain: Loss of purposeful hand skills (REQUIRED criterion)?
questions.question: Yes – loss of intentional hand use (reaching, grasping, object manipulation) is required

questions.domain: Loss of spoken language (REQUIRED criterion)?
questions.question: Yes – loss of words previously acquired; regression to babbling or silence is required

questions.domain: Regression followed by stabilization or partial recovery of skills?
questions.question: Yes – plateau/pseudo-stationary phase (Stage 3) follows regression in classic RTT

questions.domain: Stereotypic hand movements replacing purposeful hand use (REQUIRED criterion)?
questions.question: Yes – hand stereotypies required; wringing, squeezing, clapping, tapping, mouthing, or washing/rubbing automatisms

questions.domain: Stereotypies present midline (in front of body) rather than at sides?
questions.question: Yes – characteristic midline hand stereotypies; wringing/squeezing most classic pattern

questions.domain: Stereotypies present during waking hours and suppressed during sleep?
questions.question: Yes – stereotypies reduce during sleep; persist during most waking hours

sections.heading: GAIT AND MOTOR FEATURES — REQUIRED CRITERION

questions.domain: Gait dyspraxia or apraxia (REQUIRED criterion for classic RTT)?
questions.question: Yes – gait abnormality required; dyspraxic/apraxic wide-based gait in ambulatory patients

questions.domain: Unsteady or toe-walking gait?
questions.question: Yes – toe-walking, wide-based, or ataxic gait common

questions.domain: Progressive loss of ambulation over time (Stage 4)?
questions.question: Yes – many patients lose ambulation in Stage 4 (late motor deterioration)

questions.domain: Hypotonia evolving to spasticity in older patients?
questions.question: Yes – early hypotonia followed by progressive spasticity and rigidity in later stages

questions.domain: Breathing dysregulation during wakefulness (hyperventilation, breath-holding, air swallowing)?
questions.question: Yes – breathing irregularities during wakefulness are a hallmark supportive feature of RTT

questions.domain: Periods of hyperventilation alternating with apnea (Valsalva-type breathing)?
questions.question: Yes – characteristic episodic hyperventilation/apnea pattern; normal breathing during sleep

questions.domain: Forced air expulsion or aerophagia (air swallowing with abdominal distension)?
questions.question: Yes – aerophagia producing abdominal bloating; unique to RTT in this clinical context

questions.domain: Seizures or epilepsy (any type)?
questions.question: Yes – seizures in approximately 60–80% of patients; peak in Stage 2–3

questions.domain: Abnormal EEG findings (slowing, epileptiform discharges, loss of sleep spindles)?
questions.question: Yes – EEG abnormalities characteristic; progressive slowing and epileptiform activity

questions.domain: Bruxism (teeth grinding)?
questions.question: Yes – bruxism is a frequent supportive feature; often nocturnal

questions.domain: Screaming or laughing episodes without apparent cause?
questions.question: Yes – unexplained screaming/laughing spells; may mimic epileptic events

questions.domain: Decreased pain sensitivity?
questions.question: Yes – altered pain perception documented in RTT patients

questions.domain: Prolonged QTc interval on ECG?
questions.question: Yes – long QT syndrome documented; increases risk of sudden unexplained death

questions.domain: Vasomotor disturbances (cold or mottled lower extremities)?
questions.question: Yes – peripheral vasomotor abnormalities common; cold, blue/purple discolored feet

questions.domain: Cardiac rhythm abnormalities or documented arrhythmia?
questions.question: Yes – arrhythmias related to autonomic dysfunction and QT prolongation

questions.domain: Scoliosis (spinal curvature)?
questions.question: Yes – scoliosis in majority; progressive; key surveillance target

questions.domain: Short stature and low body weight?
questions.question: Yes – growth failure common; low weight, short stature

questions.domain: Small hands and feet relative to body size?
questions.question: Yes – small hands and feet are a supportive feature of RTT

questions.domain: Peripheral edema or poor peripheral circulation?
questions.question: Yes – lower limb edema and poor circulation observed in older patients

questions.domain: Chronic constipation?
questions.question: Yes – constipation is highly prevalent; often severe and requiring treatment

questions.domain: Gastroesophageal reflux or feeding difficulties?
questions.question: Yes – GERD and feeding issues common; some require G-tube placement

questions.domain: Abdominal distension (often from aerophagia)?
questions.question: Yes – bloating related to air swallowing behavioral pattern

questions.domain: Disturbed sleep-wake cycle (night laughing, screaming, agitation)?
questions.question: Yes – sleep disturbances very common; night wakening, nocturnal behavioral episodes

questions.domain: Daytime sleeping and night-time wakefulness reversal?
questions.question: Yes – circadian rhythm disruption; reversed sleep-wake pattern in subset

questions.domain: Intense eye gaze or eye pointing used as primary communication tool?
questions.question: Yes – preserved eye contact and eye pointing is characteristic of RTT; key communication channel

questions.domain: Reduced response to pain?
questions.question: Yes – decreased pain sensitivity is a recognized supportive feature

questions.domain: Brain MRI: diffuse cerebral atrophy or reduced brain volume?
questions.question: Yes – generalized cerebral atrophy on MRI; brain weight reduced vs age-matched controls

questions.domain: Brain MRI: reduced caudate nucleus volume or basal ganglia changes?
questions.question: Variable – subcortical changes in subset; substantia nigra melanin reduction described

questions.domain: Normal MRI early in disease course (does not exclude RTT)?
questions.question: Yes – MRI may appear normal in early stages; atrophy becomes apparent over time

questions.domain: De novo MECP2 mutation (no affected parent)?
questions.question: Yes – >99% of classic RTT cases arise de novo; familial cases extremely rare

questions.domain: No family history of Rett syndrome or similar condition?
questions.question: Yes – negative family history expected; consistent with de novo etiology

questions.domain: Maternal carrier testing negative (or not applicable)?
questions.question: Yes – MECP2 maternal carrier variants are possible but rare; most fathers have unaffected daughters

questions.domain: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic MECP2 variant identified on Xq28?
questions.question: Yes – MECP2 mutation found in ~95% of classic RTT; definitive diagnosis

questions.domain: Variant in methyl-CpG binding domain (MBD) — exons 3–4?
questions.question: Yes – MBD mutations (e.g., T158M, R133C, R106W) among most common and well-characterized

questions.domain: Variant in transcriptional repression domain (TRD/NID) — exon 4?
questions.question: Yes – TRD mutations (e.g., R270X, R255X, R306C) account for large proportion of cases

questions.domain: Truncating mutation (nonsense or frameshift) — generally more severe phenotype?
questions.question: Yes – truncating mutations (R168X, R270X) correlate with more severe clinical phenotype

questions.domain: MECP2 large deletion identified by MLPA/CGH array (if sequencing negative)?
questions.question: Yes – large deletions in 1–3% of RTT; requires deletion/duplication analysis beyond sequencing

questions.domain: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) pattern assessed — skewed vs. random?
questions.question: Variable – skewed XCI toward mutant allele associated with more severe phenotype

sections.heading: DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS EXCLUSIONS (Classic RTT Requires Exclusion of)

questions.domain: No brain injury from perinatal trauma, infection, or neurometabolic disease?
questions.question: Yes – acquired causes of regression excluded; no hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

questions.domain: No grossly abnormal psychomotor development in first 6 months (excludes congenital variant)?
questions.question: Yes – early development was normal; congenital onset variant RTT excluded

questions.domain: No pathogenic HNRNPH2 variant (excludes BEXS Syndrome, key RTT mimic)?
questions.question: Yes – HNRNPH2-NDD excluded; BEXS is clinically indistinguishable without sequencing

questions.domain: No pathogenic CDKL5 variant (excludes early-onset seizure variant RTT)?
questions.question: Yes – CDKL5 excluded; presents earlier with infantile spasms before regression

questions.domain: No pathogenic FOXG1 variant (excludes congenital Rett variant)?
questions.question: Yes – FOXG1 excluded; congenital variant has no normal period and earlier onset

questions.domain: No Angelman syndrome features (normal UBE3A and 15q11-q13 methylation)?
questions.question: Yes – Angelman excluded; Angelman has prominent happy affect and lacks RTT regression pattern

Classic RTT Diagnostic Criteria (Neul 2010 / RettSearch Consortium)

REQUIRED for Classic RTT (all 4 must be present):
  1. Period of regression followed by stabilization or recovery
  2. Loss of purposeful hand skills
  3. Loss of spoken language
  4. Gait abnormalities — dyspraxia or apraxia

SUPPORTIVE CRITERIA (not required but increase confidence):
  • Breathing irregularities during wakefulness (hyperventilation, breath-holding, air swallowing)
  • Bruxism, screaming/laughing spells without apparent cause
  • Impaired (not absent) communication
  • Acquired microcephaly
  • Spasticity, dystonia, scoliosis
  • Peripheral vasomotor disturbances (cold, mottled feet)
  • Sleep disturbances

EXCLUSION CRITERIA for Classic RTT:
  • Brain injury from perinatal trauma, neurometabolic disease, or severe infection
  • Grossly abnormal psychomotor development in first 6 months
  • Neurological disorder caused by identified gene mutation other than MECP2
  (Note: MECP2 mutation alone does not make the diagnosis — clinical criteria must be met)

Phase 1 — Clinical Evaluation (No Cost):
  • Comprehensive neurodevelopmental history with milestone timeline and regression documentation
  • Neurological and dysmorphology examination
  • Apply Neul 2010 criteria: confirm all 4 required criteria are met
  • Breathing pattern observation (hyperventilation, breath-holding, air swallowing during wakefulness)
  • Potential: 60–80 points for $0 if all 4 required criteria + breathing irregularities present

Phase 2 — Targeted Investigations ($300–1,500):
  • EEG — epileptiform discharges, background slowing, loss of sleep spindles
  • ECG/Holter — QTc interval assessment (long QT risk)
  • Spine X-ray — scoliosis baseline and surveillance
  • Ophthalmology evaluation
  • Additional: 10–20 points for $500–1,500

Phase 3 — Definitive Genetic Testing ($3,000–12,000+):
  • Step 1: MECP2 sequence analysis (detects ~97% of MECP2 point mutations)
  • Step 2: MECP2 MLPA/deletion analysis if sequencing negative (detects large deletions)
  • Step 3: If MECP2 negative — CDKL5, FOXG1, HNRNPH2 sequencing (RTT/Rett-mimic panel)
  • Step 4: Whole exome sequencing trio if panel negative
  • Brain MRI: cerebral atrophy, basal ganglia assessment
  • X-chromosome inactivation study if VUS identified
  • Additional: 40–55 points — crossing diagnostic threshold

• RTT IS PRIMARILY A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS based on Neul 2010 criteria — MECP2 genetic confirmation is strongly recommended but RTT can be diagnosed clinically when all 4 required criteria are met
• Prevalence: approximately 1 in 10,000–20,000 live female births; one of the most common causes of severe intellectual disability in females
• MECP2 mutations found in ~95% of classic RTT; ~5% are MECP2-negative classic RTT — these require Rett panel or WES
• Disease stage is critical context: Stage 1 (stagnation, 6–18 mo) → Stage 2 (rapid regression, 1–4 yr) → Stage 3 (pseudo-stationary, 2–10 yr) → Stage 4 (late motor deterioration)
• Breathing irregularities (hyperventilation/breath-holding during wakefulness) are among the most disease-specific features and help distinguish RTT from HNRNPH2-NDD and Angelman
• TREATMENT MILESTONE: Trofinetide (Daybue™) received FDA approval in March 2023 — first disease-specific treatment for RTT; targets IGF-1 pathway
• Cardiac surveillance mandatory: QTc prolongation increases risk of sudden unexplained death; annual ECG recommended
• Genetic counseling: de novo in >99% of cases; recurrence risk is very low (<1%) for subsequent pregnancies; germline mosaicism possible in rare cases
• HNRNPH2-NDD (BEXS Syndrome) is the most clinically similar mimic — impossible to distinguish without sequencing; both are X-linked, both present with regression, stereotypies, and language loss
Phenotypic Spectrum, Variant-Phenotype Correlations, and RTT Variants

Common Pathogenic MECP2 Variants (account for ~70% of cases):
  R168X, R270X (truncating, typically severe) | T158M, R133C, R106W (MBD missense, variable) | R255X, R294X, R306C

Genotype-Phenotype Correlations:
  • Truncating mutations in N-terminal region → more severe: earlier seizures, more profound DD
  • C-terminal truncations (R294X, R306C) → milder phenotype; better preserved speech/ambulation
  • T158M → intermediate severity; frequent in preserved speech variant
  • Skewed XCI toward mutant allele → more severe; toward wild-type → milder

Recognized RTT Variant Forms:
  • Preserved Speech Variant (PSV/Zappella) — milder; partial recovery of speech in Stage 3 (MECP2)
  • Early-Onset Seizure Variant — infantile spasms before regression (CDKL5 gene, Xp22)
  • Congenital Variant — no normal period; onset from birth (FOXG1 gene, 14q12)
  • Late Regression Variant — regression after age 3.5 years

Key Differential Diagnoses:
  • BEXS Syndrome (HNRNPH2) — closest clinical mimic; lacks breathing irregularities; no prior normal period required
  • Angelman Syndrome — happy affect, distinctive EEG, chromosome 15 abnormality
  • CDKL5-related disorder — earlier epilepsy onset, infantile spasms before regression period
  • FOXG1-related disorder — no normal period, more severe DD from birth
  • Pitt-Hopkins Syndrome (TCF4) — breathing pattern overlap (episodic hyperventilation)
  • Autism Spectrum Disorder — regression can mimic but hand stereotypies and breathing pattern distinguish RTT

confidenceNote:
🔴  85–100 points: High Confidence — Classic Rett Syndrome highly likely; genetic confirmation strongly recommended; proceed to MECP2 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis
🟡  40–84 points: Moderate Confidence — RTT probable or possible; MECP2 sequencing + deletion/duplication analysis indicated; Rett/Angelman panel and clinical genetics referral if MECP2 negative
🟢  <40 points: Low Confidence — Classic RTT unlikely; consider atypical RTT variants (CDKL5, FOXG1) or RTT mimics (HNRNPH2, Angelman)
